data.title: Midday Markets Need to Know: Steel prices surge, diesel costs stay high, and more
data.description:
Wall Street’s major market averages were mixed on Friday as technology stocks came under further pressure amid an already challenging trading week.

Here are the four news items investors should watch:

U.S. steel prices hit four-year highs: The steel sector is set to report Q3 earnings in the coming days and weeks that analysts expect will show higher sales and profits, as U.S. steel prices have climbed to more than four-year highs. U.S. tariffs on imported steel are restricting foreign supply, which has helped boost U.S. hot-rolled coil prices by 52% over the past year to $1,255/short ton, the highest level since May 2022, Bloomberg reported Friday. The U.S. is a net importer of steel but deliveries of overseas supplies have declined sharply this year, as imports of finished steel fell 14% YTD to ~13M tons, resulting in a slide of imports' share of the domestic market to 16% from 19% for the same period last year, according to the American Iron and Steel Institute.

High global diesel prices and supply constraints: High global diesel prices and supply constraints are set to persist even as crude oil prices (CL1:COM), and (CO1:COM) soften, according to Daan Struyven, Goldman Sachs co-head of global commodities research. In an interview with CNBC, Struyven noted that Goldman Sachs expects "somewhat lower crude prices" going forward but warned of "very high product prices for longer." U.S. average retail diesel prices recently hit an all-time high of $6.50 a gallon and remain just above $6, creating significant economic headwinds. Struyven described diesel as the "workhorse fuel of the global economy," explaining that unlike gasoline (XB1:COM) and jet fuel, "it has a very broad-based impact on many CPI categories."

Household debt delinquencies rise: The U.S. government isn't the only one with a debt problem. One in five Americans fell behind on a loan or mortgage payment in 2025, according to new data from the Federal Reserve that tracks the metrics every three years. That figure is up from one in eight Americans in 2022 and marks the highest level since 2007. Additionally, more than 8% of them reported being two months late or more, up from 5% in 2022. Interest rates for major types of household debt increased over the period of 2022 to 2025, with the average interest rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rising from 4.2% to 6.7% and the average new vehicle loan interest rate advancing from 4.9% to 7.7%.

Miami leads major metros in housing buyer imbalance: Miami was the strongest buyer’s market among the 10 leading U.S. metropolitan areas in September, with home sellers outnumbering buyers by 158.9%, according to Redfin data shared by Charlie Bilello. Miami had 18.9K home sellers compared with 7.3K buyers, the largest percentage gap in the ranking. Nashville, Tennessee, followed, with sellers outnumbering buyers by 152.3%, while Houston, Texas, ranked third at 134.6%. Nashville had 18.1K sellers and 7.2K buyers, while Houston recorded 47.5K sellers against 20,230 buyers. Although Houston had the largest number of sellers among the 10 markets, Miami had the widest relative gap between sellers and buyers.

data.title: Sanara MedTech/MiMedx deal spread widens on FTC second request.
data.description:
Sanara MedTech (SMTI) and MiMedx (MDXG) disclosed that they each received a request for additional information from the Federal Trade Commission over their planned combination. The deal spread widened to $1.98 from 13c on Thursday.

The companies received the second request from the FTC on Thursday, according to an  8-K filing on Friday. The effect of a second request is to extend the waiting period imposed by the HSR Act until 30 days after the parties have substantially complied with the second request.

Sanara MedTech (SMTI) said it continues to work “constructively” with the FTC in its review of the deal.

In late July, MiMedx (MDXG) agreed to buy Sanara MedTech  (SMTI) for $35 a share. Under the agreement, Sanara (SMTI) shareholders will receive $33.00 in cash and 0.4735 shares of MiMedx (MDXG) common stock for each share of Sanara common stock they own.

data.title: Moderna falls ahead of cancer vaccine data next week
data.description:
After a more than sevenfold YTD jump, Moderna (MRNA) fell nearly 10% in afternoon trading on Friday, becoming the biggest decliner in the S&P 500 (SP500) as investors await detailed results from a late-stage trial of its personalized cancer shot, intismeran autogene, developed with Merck (MRK).

The Cambridge, Massachusetts-based biotech has already lost over 5% this week, a notable reversal of fortunes for a company that skyrocketed more than 170% in a single session in August following topline data from the Phase 3 trial named INTerpath-001.

At the time, the companies said the study, which tested intismeran with Merck’s (MRK) anti-PD-1 therapy Keytruda in patients with melanoma whose tumors were completely resected, met its primary endpoint of recurrence-free survival.

The presentation scheduled for Oct. 24 at this year’s European Society for Medical Oncology Congress is expected to shed more light on INTerpath-001, which was the first trial of its kind to outperform Keytruda in an adjuvant setting for resected melanoma.

However, investors have become increasingly cautious of Moderna (MRNA) ahead of the readout, with Seeking Alpha analysts issuing multiple Hold and Sell ratings on the stock over the past few weeks. SA analyst Mike Zaccardi is the latest to issue a Hold recommendation, noting a valuation that “remains story-driven and speculative.”

data.title: NatWest withdraws markets securities business from New York Fed's primary dealers list
data.description:
NatWest Group (NWG) withdrew its markets securities business from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's list of primary dealers, Bloomberg News reported, citing the New York Fed.

The news comes amid the bank stopping its primary dealing in the U.S. and European government bond markets as NatWest seeks to simplify its markets business structure.

The new list is effective Friday.

data.title: Six Flags hits record low as fatal roller coaster raises safety concerns
data.description:
The deadly rollercoaster accident at a Six Flags (FUN) park in Georgia continues to weigh on the company’s shares, dragging FUN to an all-time low for a fourth straight day in the red.

On Monday, a 42-year-old man fell to his death after being ejected from his seat while on the Goliath hypercoaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. Four children were also injured at the time with non-life-threatening injuries.

The cause of the accident remains under investigation, so it is still too early to determine if it was due to mechanical failure or operational error. As a precaution, Six Flags (FUN) closed nine rollercoasters in six parks.

While this will have some impact on park attendance, the direct impact on the company’s profit and loss will depend on whether the investigation points to a systemic restraint/design issue or safety failure, UBS advises its clients.

“A key risk for Six Flags is reputational spillover into attendance and pass sales at a time when leverage already limits the company’s ability to absorb a demand shock,” notes UBS analyst Arpine Kocharyab, adding that these types of events are “rare idiosyncratic events” that are unlikely to have a sustained attendance or EBITDA impact.

“Until the investigation establishes root cause, we would view reputational/attendance risk as potentially greater than the direct cost of the Georgia incident itself,” Kocharyab says.

Still, the reputational risk is amplified by a series of events that raise questions over the safety of Six Flags’ (FUN) rollercoasters.

The parks have been hit with complaints over injuries (some as serious as concussions and dislocated joints), malfunctioning safety restraints, and shoddy maintenance.

In September, a lawsuit representing 100 plaintiffs claims the X2 rollercoaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in California is linked to numerous injuries, including traumatic brain injuries, and was behind the death of a 22-year-old in June 2022. The lawsuit claims the extreme mechanics of the ride—including 76 mph speed, extreme G-force, and violent jolting—caused the riders’ heads to slam repeatedly against the headrests.

According to an investor lawsuit filed against Six Flags (FUN), the company was accused of "failing to make adequate investments to conduct routine facility maintenance or improve rides,” while another federal class-action lawsuit accuses Six Flags’ (FUN) management of misleading shareholders regarding deferred maintenance and the actual condition of its parks leading into its 2024 merger with Cedar Fair.

Even before the most recent tragic accident, shares of Six Flags (FUN) were losing ground and have lost more than 60% in value from a year ago.

data.title: Formula One price target cut to $110 at Susquehanna
data.description:
Susquehanna International Group lowered its price target on Formula One (FWONK) to $110 from $114, citing lower market multiples, while maintaining its positive rating and revenue and EBITDA estimates.

The new target implies about 21% upside from the stock's last close.

Formula One (FWONK) and TKO Group Holdings (TKO) have fallen 8% and 16%, respectively, year to date, underperforming the broader sports and entertainment sector amid investor concerns over Middle Eastern event exposure.

Analyst Joseph Stauff said the potential cancellation of scheduled events remains a notable risk amid the Iran conflict, despite management’s stated intention to proceed. Formula One (FWONK) is scheduled to hold races in Qatar on November 29 and Abu Dhabi on December 6.

The analyst estimates third-quarter consolidated revenue of $1.19 billion and EBITDA of $327 million, broadly in line with its prior expectations. They also said Formula One’s planned increase in sprint races to 10 from six in 2027 could support growth through sponsor and promoter demand and higher viewership.

Stauff identified deteriorating engagement trends and a prolonged Iran conflict into 2027 as downside risks, with a downside scenario of $85.

data.title: Regions Financial trades higher after strong Q3 earnings, revenue beats
data.description:
Regions Financial (RF) stock increased 1.7% in Friday midday trading after the regional bank posted strong beats on Q3 earnings and revenue as its provision for credit losses came in lower than expected. The company also reaffirmed its full-year  guidance.

The bank still expects full-year net interest income growth of 2.5%-4%, net interest margin exiting the year at ~3.7%, adjusted noninterest income growth of 3%-5%, and adjusted noninterest expense growth of 1.5%-3.5%. Regions (RF) continues to expect to generate adjusted operating leverage in 2026.

Q4 NII is expected to increase 1%-2% from Q3 2026, implying $1.33B-$1.34B (vs. S&P CapIQ consensus of $1.33B). It also projects Q4 NIM at ~3.70%, in line with prior guidance.

Q3 non-GAAP EPS of $0.73, topping the consensus estimate of $0.66, rose/fell from $0.68 in Q2 and $0.63 in Q3 2025.

Q3 adjusted revenue of $1.97B, beating the average analyst estimate of $1.83B, increased from $1.95B in the prior quarter and $1.94B a year ago.

"Strong credit quality, continued momentum in fee-based businesses, and economically vibrant markets throughout our footprint all contributed to our third quarter results," said Chairman, President, and CEO John Turner.

NII (FTE) of $1.31B, vs. the S&P CapIQ consensus of $1.31B, climbed from $1.29B in Q2 and $1.27B in last year’s Q3.

Its net interest margin (FTE) of 3.68%, vs. the 3.67% S&P CapIQ consensus, improved from 3.66% in the previous quarter and 3.59% a year ago.

Region Financial's (RF) provision for credit losses of $68M, vs. the S&P CapIQ consensus of $116M, was flat with Q2 and declined from $105M in last year’s Q3.

Average loans stood at $99.2B vs. $98.7B in Q2. Average deposits of $129.1B dipped from $130.7B in the prior quarter.

Adjusted return on tangible common equity improved to 21.66% from 20.18% in the previous quarter and 19.24% in the year-ago period.

data.title: Loop outlines 45,000-tonne India plant, targets construction start in Q1 2027 and completion by end of 2028
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Loop Industries (LOOP) Q2 2027

Management View

  • “Our Indian joint venture with Ester Industries has made the decision to reduce the capacity of the first facility in India from 70,000 kilotonnes (sic) [ tonnes ] to 45,000 kilotonnes (sic) [ tonnes ] per annum.” (Founder, President, CEO & Director Daniel Solomita)
  • “This change will significantly lower the capital cost of the facility and the resulting debt and equity financing needs.” (CEO Solomita)
  • “If we are successful in raising our capital, we would expect to begin construction in Q1 calendar of 2027 and complete construction by the end of 2028.” (CEO Solomita)
  • “We are engaged in positive discussions with a major bank in India... These discussions are progressing well.” (CEO Solomita)
  • “We successfully completed the technology assessment of the TEV study, and that will be used by the debt lender as documentation for their loan for the debt piece in India.” (CEO Solomita)
  • “Our cash operating expenses for the quarter were $1.6 million, a year-over-year reduction of $800,000, and our run rate has continued to decline into the third quarter.” (Independent CFO, Principal Accounting Officer & Director Spencer Hart)
  • “As of August 31, we reported total available liquidity of $1.9 million.” (CFO Hart)
  • “To address our capital needs... our Board formed a special committee in September of 2026.” (CFO Hart)

Outlook

  • “The Indian facility is still contemplated to be the first of 2 facilities on the same site. The second facility is planned to be substantially larger than the first 1 and would follow after a successful start-up of the first facility.” (CEO Solomita)
  • “The time for construction, start-up and commissioning is a total of 20 months.” (CEO Solomita)
  • “If the funding is secured and we start the project in beginning of 2027 calendar year, we would have the plant up and running commercially producing material by the end of 2028.” (CEO Solomita)
  • The transcript did not include EPS or revenue guidance, and the analysts estimates JSON did not meet the provided validation format requirements (quarter not labeled as Q1–Q4), so no estimates comparison is included.

Financial Results

  • “We have maintained a strong focus on cost control, and that's allowed us to reduce our overhead.” (CFO Hart)
  • “These savings reflect targeted reductions in personnel, insurance and other operating expenses, as well as the waiver of cash compensation by our outside directors.” (CFO Hart)
  • “Importantly, rescaling our first commercial facility in India will reduce the project's overall capital requirements, directly lowering our required equity contribution.” (CFO Hart)

Q&A

  • Jon Hickman, Ladenburg Thalmann & Co. Inc., Research Division: “Could you give us an estimate for the revised total cost of the project... and what the new equity contribution is?” CEO Solomita: “We don't have the final number yet... But it will be significantly lower than the 70,000-tonne plant that we had initially.”
  • Jon Hickman, Ladenburg Thalmann & Co. Inc., Research Division: “So you think you can get the funding put together...?” CEO Solomita: “...we would have the plant up and running commercially producing material by the end of 2028.”
  • Jon Hickman, Ladenburg Thalmann & Co. Inc., Research Division: “...have you talked to interested parties already?” CFO Hart: “We're engaged with advisers and actively working in discussions... we can't promise anything until it's done.”
  • Gerard Sweeney, ROTH Capital Partners, LLC, Research Division: “...does this impact anything around the debt financing...?” CEO Solomita: “It is only viewed as a positive by the debt lenders.”
  • Gerard Sweeney, ROTH Capital Partners, LLC, Research Division: “...any other areas that you're pursuing alternatively...?” CFO Hart: “We're very flexible in terms of the form of the capital that we're raising.”
  • Gerard Sweeney, ROTH Capital Partners, LLC, Research Division: “...any time lines when you think...?” CFO Hart: “...we're just not going to do is predict exactly how much or when... in order to break ground in the first quarter of next year, we have to have the financing in place in advance of that.”
  • Marvin Wolff, Paradigm Capital: “...what percent of that do you have contracted out?” CEO Solomita: “...we are over a threshold of 50% of the facility sold.”
  • Marvin Wolff, Paradigm Capital: “...does that imply a larger second plant?” CEO Solomita: “...we would be able to grow the second facility to 125,000 tonnes.”
  • Marvin Wolff, Paradigm Capital: “...downsized amount can be just as profitable...?” CEO Solomita: “...in India... it doesn't impact our financials dramatically. So it's still very profitable.”
  • Varyk Kutnick, Divyde Capital Partners L.P.: “...shouldn't your equity contribution be somewhere near like $12 million now?” CFO Hart: “...it seems realistic to think that they'll finance 70% of the project... our portion is about 15% of the total project cost... we have made a portion already... It's in the kind of $3 million to $5 million range.”

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts slightly negative to pressing on financing certainty and timing, including “a little bit of friction here, I think, securing some financing” (Gerard Sweeney, ROTH Capital Partners, LLC, Research Division) and repeated requests for cost/equity specifics.
  • Management slightly positive but cautious on fundraising specificity, including “we can't promise anything until it's done” (CFO Hart) and “we don't have the final number yet” (CEO Solomita), paired with confidence statements such as “We're very confident” (CEO Solomita) regarding lender reception and offtake support.
  • Versus the prior quarter, the current call’s language placed more emphasis on capital-raising uncertainty and process controls (special committee), while the prior quarter emphasized project momentum in India and Europe and expectations for engineering-related cash flow.

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Q2 shifted the India plan to a smaller first facility: “reduce the capacity... to 45,000” (CEO Solomita) versus Q1 discussion centered on a 70,000-ton plant and breaking ground in “the fall of this year” (CEO Solomita, prior quarter).
  • Q2 introduced governance around financing: “our Board formed a special committee in September of 2026” (CFO Hart) whereas Q1 described evaluating financing options without referencing a committee.
  • Q2 commentary focused tightly on India debt/equity mechanics and TEV technical diligence, while Q1 included detailed Europe licensing/engineering milestones and expected cash inflows tied to Societe Generale (prior quarter).
  • Analyst focus remained consistent on offtake coverage, funding mix, and timing, with Q2 questions pressing for revised capex/equity amounts following the rescale.

Risks and Concerns

  • “Notwithstanding the current low stock price and our efforts on raising the capital required for the facility...” (CEO Solomita)
  • “...we can't promise anything until it's done.” (CFO Hart)
  • “We don't have the final number yet.” (CEO Solomita)

Final Takeaway

Loop’s management framed Q2 around rescaling the first India facility to 45,000 tonnes to lower capital needs and accelerate the timeline, while describing progressing lender technical diligence and stating that more than 50% of the downsized plant was supported by LOIs and contracts. Management also emphasized liquidity of $1.9 million as of August 31, reduced quarterly cash operating expenses of $1.6 million, and the formation of a board special committee to pursue equity, debt, and nondilutive financing to reach construction, targeting a Q1 calendar 2027 start and commercial production by end of 2028.
